deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page belongs to the same 'Litt. E' work as the previous page, which computed the Sun's place for the 3rd and 4th observations and began reducing comparison stars ('Bestimmung der Fixsterne'). It is the reduction stage of a comet-orbit computation; the orbit itself is computed on the next page. The epoch of the observations follows from the precession interval. On the previous page Gauss writes 1772.229 = 1800 − 27.771. The four observation dates (March 26.378305, 27.371844, 30.387366 and 'March 34.398582' = April 3) therefore lie in 1772. The comet of 1772 (Montaigne/Messier) is the natural candidate. That comet was later linked with the comet of 1805, i.e. Biela's comet. This identification is my inference and is not stated on the page.

A. REDUCTION OF COMPARISON STARS (7 Mon, 11 Mon, an unnamed star in Monoceros). For each star:

(i) Catalogue place (alpha_1800, delta_1800). Gauss subtracts precession over t = 27.771 yr, using linear annual rates:
  Delta alpha = t (m + n sin alpha tan delta)
  Delta delta = t n cos alpha
  with log n = 1.30116 (n ≈ 20.006") and m = 45.8817".

7 Mon:
  log n + log|cos alpha| = 1.30116 + 8.61307 = 9.91423; + log t (1.44359) gives 22.79".
  log n + log sin alpha + log tan delta = 1.30116 + 9.99963 + 9.13373 = 0.43452, i.e. 2.7197 (negative, since delta < 0).
  m − 2.7197 = 43.162 (log 1.63510); × 27.771 = 1198.64" = 19'58.64".
  Result: alpha = 92°31'12.2" − 19'58.64" = 92°11'13.56"; delta = −7°44'54.70" + 22.79" = −7°44'31.91".

11 Mon (same scheme):
  RA rate 45.8817 − 2.4160 = 43.4657 (log 1.63815); × t = 20'7.08".
  Dec: 10^(0.20638 + 1.44359) = 44.66".
  Result: 94°26'39.62", −6°54'6.44".

Unnamed star:
  log sin alpha should be 9.99093; this makes 1.30116 + 9.99093 + 9.14280 = 0.43489, i.e. 2.722.
  45.8817 − 2.722 = 43.160 (log 1.63508); × t = 19'58.59".
  Dec: 10^(0.60712 + 1.44359) = 1'52.39".
  Result: 101°30'32.06", −7°53'38.41".

(ii) Annual aberration (constant k = 20"). Gauss introduces auxiliaries H and h (my notation):
  tan H = tan(sun) / cos eps
  h = k sqrt(cos^2(sun) cos^2(eps) + sin^2(sun))
  For the Sun at 10°41' this gives H = 10°41' + 56' = 11°37' and log h = 1.2649 (h ≈ 18.41"). For April 3 (Sun 14°38'): H = 15°53', log h = 1.2662.
  Then:
  Delta alpha = −h cos(alpha − H) sec delta. For 7 Mon: 1.2649n + 9.2146 + 0.0040 = 0.4835n, i.e. −3.04". For 11 Mon −2.31"; unnamed star −1.42".
  Delta delta = h sin(alpha − H) sin delta. For 7 Mon: 1.2649n + 9.9941n + 9.1294n = 0.3884n, i.e. −2.45". For 11 Mon −2.19"; unnamed star −2.53".
  The remaining declination term −k sin eps cos(sun) cos delta is split as
   −(k sin eps / 2)[cos(sun − delta) + cos(sun + delta)], with k sin eps / 2 ≈ 3.98.
  This gives the bracketed pairs: (3.98, 3.78) for 7 Mon; (3.97, 3.80) for 11 Mon; (3.95, 3.68) for the unnamed star.

(iii) Nutation.
  Moon's node: Omega = 7s 0°3' = 210°3' (March 30); 6s 29°51' (April 3), a 12' regression in 4 days.
  Auxiliary argument A = Omega − 6°34' = 203°29' (203°28' on April 3). Amplitude log N = 0.9549n (N ≈ −9.01").
  Delta alpha = C + N cos(A − alpha) tan delta, where C = +8.27" (≈ Delta psi cos eps with Delta psi ≈ 18" × 0.50). C becomes 8.22" on April 3, scaling with sin Omega.
  Delta delta = N sin(A − alpha).
  7 Mon: A − alpha = 111°18'. RA term: 0.9549n + 9.5602n + 9.1334n = 9.6485n, i.e. −0.45". Dec term: 0.9549n + 9.9693 = 0.9242n, i.e. −8.40".
  11 Mon: A − alpha = 109°2'. RA term −0.36"; Dec term −8.52".
  Unnamed star: A − alpha = 101°57'. RA term −0.26"; Dec term −8.82".

Apparent places:
  7 Mon: 13.56 − 3.04 − 0.45 + 8.27 → 92°11'18.34"; 31.91 + 2.45 + 3.98 + 3.78 + 8.40 → −7°44'50.52".
  11 Mon: 39.62 − 2.31 − 0.36 + 8.27 → 94°26'45.22"; −6°54'24.92".
  Unnamed star: 32.06 − 1.42 − 0.26 + 8.22 → 101°30'38.60"; −7°53'57.39".

B. OBSERVATION TABLE. For each date Gauss lists:
- time (days of March 1772);
- Sun's longitude: 6°43'52", 7°42'44", 10°41'11", 14°38'6" (rate ≈ 59'/day, consistent);
- log R: 9.999573, 9.999704, 0.0000?1, 0.000597;
- the comet's apparent (alpha, delta), e.g. 90°11'51.20", −7°6'21.72".
Each (alpha, delta) is converted to ecliptic (lambda, beta) and log tan beta, using obliquity eps = 23°28'2.83". Gauss's standard auxiliary-angle method:
  tan N = tan delta / sin alpha
  tan lambda = tan alpha cos(N − eps) / cos N (computed as cot lambda = cot alpha · cos N / cos(N − eps), since lambda ≈ 90°)
  tan beta = tan(N − eps) sin lambda

Obs. 1:
  9.0957394 − 9.9999974 = 9.0957420, so N = 7°6'21.87"; N + eps = 30°34'24.70" (south).
  log cot lambda = 7.5375683 + 0.0616546 = 7.5992229, so lambda = 90°13'39.69".
  log tan beta = 9.7714220 + 9.9999966 = 9.7714186, so beta = −30°34'24.00".
The other three observations, done the same way:
  91°49'8.89", −30°41'54.69"
  96°37'43.84", −31°3'7.40"
  102°55'16.29", −31°11'21.14"
The log cos delta, log cos beta, log sec delta columns are control/auxiliary quantities (e.g. for cos delta cos alpha = cos beta cos lambda). These lambda, beta, log tan beta (marked n on the next page) feed the next page's parabolic-orbit computation (Olbers-type ratio M, then i, Omega, omega).
errors: 7 Mon declination: the transcribed terms (−2.45, −3.93, −3.78, −8.40) sum to 50.47", not the 50.52" written. With the aberration term computed as 3.98·cos(sun+delta) ≈ 3.98 the sum is exactly 50.52". The manuscript digit is almost certainly 3.98 (misread), so no real error.

11 Mon RA: the transcription's terms (−2.31, +8.36) do not give 45.22". Gauss's own log computation gives a nutation term −0.36", and with −2.31 − 0.36 + 8.27 the result 45.22" is exact. This is a transcription merge, not a Gauss error.
Unnamed star: Gauss writes the log tan delta factor (9.1419) without the 'n' sign mark, yet correctly takes the product as negative (9.4131n → −0.26"). This is a notational slip only.

Unnamed star: the RA-precession log sin alpha transcribed as 9.99404 is inconsistent with the stated sum 0.43489. The correct value 9.99093 = log sin 101.6° reproduces it, so the error is in the transcription.

log R for March 30 is transcribed 0.000031. The previous page gives 0.0000912, and interpolation between the neighbouring values gives ≈0.000091. Either a misreading or a copying slip on Gauss's part; it does not affect the lambda, beta reductions.
The aberration amplitude log 1.2649 vs a recomputed 1.2652 (k = 20") differs by about 0.0003 in the log. This is negligible (< 0.02" in the corrections).
Otherwise every checked log sum, sexagesimal addition and conversion (including the recomputed lambda for observation 2, 1°49'8.9" past 90°) agrees to within 0.1".

results.what: Reduction of catalogue star places back 27.771 years by linear annual precession: Delta alpha = t(m + n sin alpha tan delta), Delta delta = t n cos alpha, with m = 45.8817", n ≈ 20.006"
results.modern_name: Precession in right ascension and declination (first-order annual-variation formulae)

results.what: Annual aberration in alpha, delta written compactly with auxiliary angle H (tan H = tan sun / cos eps) and amplitude h; constant dec term split into two cosines
results.modern_name: Annual aberration in equatorial coordinates (auxiliary-angle form, cf. Besselian day numbers)
results.usually_credited_to: Bradley (aberration, 1729); trigonometric reduction forms by Euler, Lalande, later Bessel

results.what: Nutation in alpha, delta with constant term Delta psi cos eps plus a combined periodic term N cos(A − alpha) tan delta and N sin(A − alpha), with A = Omega − 6°34'
results.modern_name: Nutation corrections (Bradley/Mayer–Maskelyne ellipse model) in compact auxiliary form

results.what: Conversion of apparent alpha, delta to ecliptic lambda, beta via auxiliary angle N: tan N = tan delta / sin alpha, tan lambda = tan alpha cos(N − eps)/cos N, tan beta = tan(N − eps) sin lambda
results.usually_credited_to: Classical spherical astronomy; this formulation appears in Gauss's Theoria Motus (1809)

deep.surprise_reason: Purely routine reduction work for a comet orbit: precession, aberration and nutation of comparison stars, then equatorial-to-ecliptic conversion, all by standard methods Gauss is well known to have used. The only historically interesting aspect is the probable identification of the material as the 1772 comet observations (connected to Gauss's 1805-06 work on the comet later called Biela's). That is documentary context, not a new mathematical result.
